splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan must be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or can be selected afterward. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, preventing individuals from running out the clock on their supervision period by fleeing.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend punishment beyond statutory terms without explicit congressional authorization.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face an additional gatekeeping requirement under § 2244(b)(1) when bringing successive collateral attacks. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements. The split affects the ability of federal prisoners to seek post-conviction relief.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h) requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split affects whether election rules can be challenged before elections take place or only afterward, with significant implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury when state laws alter the rules under which their elections are conducted, granting them standing to challenge such laws before an election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in election rules being followed does not constitute a concrete, particularized injury sufficient for Article III standing without a showing of specific harm.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bognet v. Secretary Commonwealth of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) in construing ambiguous provisions of the Sentencing Guidelines that increase criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference in the criminal sentencing context.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as one of the oldest canons of interpretation, takes priority over deference to agency or Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, permitting courts to adopt anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions based on the Commission's commentary.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 (which includes conspiracy) exceeds the Commission's interpretive authority under Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is entitled to deference under Kisor. Some circuits defer to the commentary while others hold the guideline text is unambiguous and excludes inchoate offenses. This affects career-offender sentencing enhancements for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text is ambiguous regarding inchoate offenses and Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy is a reasonable interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Kisor/Stinson deference.

positions.label: Commentary is not entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b)'s text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses because it does not mention conspiracy, attempt, or aiding and abetting, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) or whether possessing any single criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' effectively means 'or,' so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule of controlled substances is broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law, or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on the federal schedule.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal limitation
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is also controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also federally controlled, requiring a match between state and federal drug schedules.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De La Rosa

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked 25-year sentences under § 924(c) — can support compassionate release motions. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others allow them as part of the analysis. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to resolve this by allowing such claims, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly when combined with other factors, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizing such consideration is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and a subsequent conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that post-petition appreciation inures to the estate, creating a split with circuits that have interpreted § 348(f)(1)(A) to protect debtors' equity gains upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors' post-petition equity gains, so post-petition appreciation does not become part of the Chapter 7 estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (subject to the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration) must proceed under habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims under Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges to conditions or execution of confinement, or whether prisoners may alternatively use civil rights statutes. This split has evolved over decades and affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions, including First Step Act time-credit determinations.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration/execution challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP execution-of-sentence decisions, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights claims may proceed alongside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that conditions-of-confinement claims and certain execution-of-sentence challenges may proceed under civil rights statutes (Bivens, APA, or § 1983) even when habeas might also be available.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Carmona v. U.S. Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant at a supervised release revocation hearing for the conduct that violated the conditions of supervision, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether district courts may impose revocation sentences that are expressly intended to punish the defendant for the violation conduct. The Sixth Circuit, under its precedent in United States v. Lewis, permits courts to expressly punish at revocation, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must be grounded in the breach of trust and the goals of supervised release, not retribution for the underlying violation.

positions.label: Courts may punish for violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct that violated supervised release conditions, allowing retribution as a sentencing consideration at revocation hearings.

positions.label: Courts may not punish for violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be based on the breach of the court's trust and the purposes of supervised release, not as punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the denial of a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. This creates tension with circuits that have taken a narrower view of what privacy interests qualify for immediate appeal under Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that the denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because parties have adequate means to vindicate privacy interests through other protective mechanisms or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions regarding fair treatment standards, discrimination liability, and damages in the hospitality and service industries. The grant suggests a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for such claims.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied standards for discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a distinctive approach to liability and remedies.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the disagreement that prompted Supreme Court review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
